We focus on three things: simplicity, automation, and cost-effectiveness. Nate needed very basic automated emails — abandoned carts in line, win-back campaigns for customers he hadn't seen in a while — so he partnered with an old friend who's an online marketing executive and built the tool. Nate started using it, had success, others in the market wanted it, and fast forward to today we're in 120 locations, growing steadily, working with a lot of top cannabis agencies that own the retailer relationship. We know we're a tool in the toolkit — we don't have to own every customer relationship. CanVersions is a great, simple, automated, set-and-forget email marketing solution for dispensaries, and we're planning to expand the feature set based on what our customers tell us.

Bryan Fields: My favorite part of that story is that it's twofold — one, he built the tool for himself first because he had a problem and recognized no solution existed, and people with the same problem started using it; and two, the simplicity of it, being able to hop in with a minimal learning curve given everyone's wearing so many hats. If he'd needed a two-week learning curve, half the building would be on fire by the time he got started.

Rick Bashkoff: And especially in marketing, cannabis is one of the first places that gets cut as the industry ebbs and flows. If you set up an entire team or system and then the marketing manager moves on, you lose that whole knowledge base and have to start over. With automated, simple tools, they don't experience that downturn as the company ebbs and flows, and you can keep your tech stack in line if you keep things simple and interoperable — we integrate directly with menu providers and other email providers to avoid double-messaging, keeping things transparent. Customers really lean into that. Nate and the team found an interesting use case and sprinted to take care of it.

Kellen Finney: Do you have to deal with different state regulations from a marketing perspective — I know some states you can't put up billboards. How does that factor into launching in a new state and maintaining across states?

Rick Bashkoff: For the most part, with email marketing there's a set of best practices that gets you to a common-denominator compliance thread — it's not as difficult as compliance differences for security or hard assets. There's a variety of best practices around messaging in email templates that encourage staying within compliance, but it's a challenge — it's an ever-changing landscape. I'm in New York and could do a whole episode on what's wrong with the marketing regulations here. My biggest frustration is that we talk about education being the tip of the spear for pushing the industry forward and decreasing Reefer Madness thinking, but regulators are handcuffing marketing and advertising — those two things competing is very frustrating for someone like me trying to normalize the plant and bring people into the regulated market instead of the illicit one. I'm not the person who should be in rooms doing advocacy with politicians, that's its own skill, but the people who do it are starting to realize the connection: how are we supposed to compete with the illicit market if we can't message the community? I'm hopeful that next time we chat this won't be as much of an issue, but right now it's the thorn in the side of any cannabis marketer.

Kellen Finney: Let's keep it going with Lit Alerts — tell us the USP for Lit Alerts and who should be thinking about applying it to their business.

Rick Bashkoff: One of the reasons we're excited about Lit Alerts is it's much more broadly applicable — use cases for brands, wholesalers, retailers, even some straight-up cultivators. Nate and Cody had CanVersions going and were looking at what's next, and the problem they went after is wholesalers, brands, and retailers not having real-time data to make critical in-market decisions. Others have attacked this problem, but our approach is different: our data source is actually retailer websites, dispensary menus. We built a crawler, not unlike Google, that goes out and looks at menus almost every hour these dispensaries are open — a tremendous amount of data ingested hourly. We compare the differences between menu snapshots to infer market activity — low quantity, out-of-stocks, pricing changes, all the sales enablement and competitive intelligence tactics sellers and field marketers are trying to replicate manually. Earlier this year our co-founders brought on an initial group of customers to validate the data set, since we're making inferences from menu snapshots — walking the data into buyer meetings to get a signal on accuracy. Our CTO and co-founder Austin built a tool that was dangerously close out of the gate, so by around October we had our first paying customers, and growth has been great — we're at 40 active customers currently with a very active pipeline, and we're getting to the point of being overwhelmed, which means we're doing something right. Within Lit Alerts you can add your own brand or a competitor's brand to what we call the Brands Explorer, sifting through menu listings — pricing, imaging, categories — for real competitive intelligence.

Bryan Fields: Can you give us an example with a brand?

Rick Bashkoff: Sure — let's say you're Miss Grass and trying to get a retail chain to replace a competitor. You put that competitor into your Brand Explorer, and now you can track their activity at that dispensary in a simple, filterable tabular view showing all the menu items we're seeing in market — pricing, where they're carried, whether they're close to selling out. As head of sales at Miss Grass, you can walk that into the wholesale meeting and say, 'This is what we're seeing in market, we think we can fill this need for you.' On the flip side, if Miss Grass tells a dispensary they're in 70 dispensaries in the state, the retailer can check that in the tool and verify it. There's a lot on both sides — democratizing the data so everyone's looking at the same thing and competing on customer needs and quality of product. We were surprised by the distribution of use cases between brands and retailers — Cody, Nate, and Austin originally thought this was mainly a brand and wholesaler tool, but retailers immediately said this is exactly what they need for competitive intelligence, so we pivoted to release retailer-specific features. We've got something cool coming — like buying an iPhone where you compare models, we're building a UI where you can compare cannabis brands or retailer locations, so a dispensary in Springfield, Massachusetts could add the four other dispensaries within a 10-mile radius and keep an ongoing leaderboard on product mix, pricing, velocity, and more.

Bryan Fields: It seems like one of the biggest challenges your team is solving is the accuracy of the data, because informed decisions rely on a data set you can trust — otherwise you're flying blind. Going back to the Miss Grass example, instead of making phone calls and taking a leap of faith, you can see on a dashboard that a product is flying in Arizona and Florida with similar demographics and know to prioritize it.

Rick Bashkoff: I want to highlight that our data set is meant to be tactical, not for financial reconciliation — it's a real-time signal. One of our co-founders, Cody, calls one of our screens an activity feed where you can see everything happening with your brand in market in real time — 'This is Twitter for cannabis wholesale.' If you're using a tool like Lit Alerts for real-time signal and backing it up with financial reconciliation at month's end, you get a great read on your markets and can evaluate strategy far more often than waiting for a single monthly report. When I first joined the team around September or October, I asked about seeing historical data from nine months ago, and everyone laughed — nobody using this tool cares about nine months ago, that's ancient history to sellers and field marketers. Menu items from six months ago often aren't even live anymore. That recency is what's powerful, along with the fact that it's dead simple to get in and out of the tool and pull data — simple views people are used to working with — creating transparency in conversations and helping deals get done quicker.

Bryan Fields: Was that always the intention from the founders when they launched it?

Rick Bashkoff: One hundred percent. Our cheat code is Nate's operations experience and network, Cody's hustle, and Austin's brain as CTO — putting those three skill sets together to make operators in cannabis feel more informed. If you're a seller with information to make decisions, that's game-changing. We hear from customers that up until using Lit Alerts they were flying blind on a lot of decisions. This isn't an app built for time spent — we're trying to affect outcomes. We named it Lit Alerts for a reason: the goal is a customizable alert system that brings you the information you need. We don't dream of everyone logging in every morning — if I get an email highlighting low-quantity and out-of-stock retailers, that's a real problem solved, saving hours of Google searching, menu-checking, and phone calls. There are other solutions like Headset Bridge, and if you have the budget and clout to get retailers to opt in their data, that works too, but it's not as complete as our real-time data set. Making tools interoperable and affordable within budget is really important to us.

Bryan Fields: I know you're also an investor in a few companies — can you give a shout-out to some of them, and for founders building in cannabis looking for an investor like yourself, what are you looking for?

Rick Bashkoff: Sure, quickly — I started a group called Receptive Capital Syndicate, now 103 accredited investors, looking at the earliest-stage cannabis companies on the East Coast, mainly IP-driven companies — brands, software companies, R&D companies. We don't invest in cultivation or retail; our checks aren't big enough to do the damage necessary there. Our portfolio includes Cantrip, a great cannabis beverage company out of Massachusetts, Miss Grass, and a company called Trym — I'd put them in this group even though they've been around a while, focused on simplicity, automation, and being good at one thing; we've been impressed with their progress on cultivation software. Grit is number one on our list — we need to see that you've gotten around a lot of tough problems, because in cannabis it's not week one, it's the first minute you'll hit a challenge you didn't see coming. One founder we got far down the line with had a bunch of past projects that weren't necessarily successful, but the story of how they got around obstacles showed us they had the ability. Revenue-producing matters too — we're not looking at pre-launch pitches. It's 2024, get your product out, get something done, then raise money. The minute you take on external capital, you work for someone else, even though that sounds crazy — you've got another voice saying chase this, look at this. Hold out as long as you can; it's not easy to bootstrap, ask Nate, Cody, and Austin, but if you can launch your product, book revenue, and have a story to tell, that matters, because the days of raising off a deck are over — probably not coming back in our lifetime. Someone recently compared themselves to Facebook or Airbnb, and that pitch is the wrong decade — capital isn't looking for those stories right now, and a lot of those companies never made money anyway. KPIs I hear from investors I respect are shifting from TAM and capture to profitability and manageable growth; hockey-stick growth is starting to become a red flag in pitches.

Bryan Fields: I think that's so important, and I appreciate you sharing that for people who had a different perception of what they needed to do.

Rick Bashkoff: I'll add — across all our investments, at the end of the day we're investing in the people, the jockey. Even with product and revenue in place, when we looked at Trym, the operating group there is no joke, they've done this in another industry. Adam and Dylan from Cantrip are seasoned operators for how young they are. And nobody's doing better than Kate at Miss Grass. There's no middle ground when you step into these deals from a founder perspective — either they've got it, or you're not getting the feel. I'd encourage entrepreneurs to find their grit and expose it as part of the process, because that's what people are looking for now. Ideas themselves are cheap — the three of us could come up with a hundred right now, and nowadays you can spit some fire into ChatGPT and get a website and a PowerPoint out of it.

Bryan Fields: What is the most expensive lesson you've ever learned?

Rick Bashkoff: You've got to be on the same page with the people you're working with daily — that's been a really expensive lesson for me. I like to think I'm a decent judge of people, but I've definitely been wrong, and it hurts when that happens. When evaluating opportunities in cannabis, spend time with the people you'll be working with before you jump in if you can — get a hiring manager or founder out for a coffee, a drink, or smoke a joint with them and get a sense of what makes them tick. A lot of hiring, investing, and deal activity in cannabis happens fast out of necessity — running out of money, exploding growth — so it's not always possible, but the most expensive things in my career have definitely been aligning myself with the wrong people.

Bryan Fields: What question do you wish more people asked you?

Rick Bashkoff: I wish more people asked me why I'm in cannabis. I got that question a lot when I first got into the industry, and it was a good reminder — I got into cannabis out of pure interest and passion. My wife makes fun of me because I spend every waking moment outside my full-time job reading or talking about cannabis. That question's kind of gone away as the industry matures, and I miss it — I miss talking about the medical aspects, use cases of hemp, the difference between things. When I got into this space, every cannabis beverage I tried tasted disgusting, like a hundred-milligram beverage that tasted like weed — and I'm a joint smoker, I love the smell of weed, but I don't want to drink a beverage that tastes like it. Seeing how the industry has progressed changes some of the reasons you're in it.

Kellen Finney: I think it's perfect, there's no right answer. To piggyback on the beverage point and give Adam a shout-out at Cantrip — the first time I gave someone that beverage, they asked if there was weed in it, I said yes, they asked if they'd get high, I said yes, and the confusion on their face was spectacular. I think that's the paradox of opening people up to what's coming.

Rick Bashkoff: My mother-in-law, if I asked her to smoke a joint with me every day for the rest of her life, the answer would be no — she drinks Cantrip. But for real, the same reason I lean forward on beverage is that I was walking through a grocery store and thought there's never going to be flower here, never pre-rolls, never gummies, but there's an entire regulated beverage section sitting there waiting to be disrupted, full of ugly Bud Light cans. I think beverage is going to be the equalizer at some point — a lot of it comes down to supply chain issues at this point, but it's an interesting dynamic between the hemp business and the cannabis business, which is really one business, joking on everyone.

Bryan Fields: Prediction time, Rick — with tools like ChatGPT becoming widely used, will companies look to integrate more software team members into their core foundation as a startup?

Rick Bashkoff: I think it's going to be more about partnering with the right tool sets, like Lit Alerts and CanVersions, rather than bringing that in-house. If you look at the cannabis brands and retailers doing really well, they focus on selling weed, not building software tools or hiring people to build them — they focus on people who can grow, produce, and sell weed really well. Let nerds like me focus on the software tools you need. I don't see cannabis companies hiring software employees; I see them buddying up with software companies and recognizing that software is the game-changer for differentiating in a maturing market — how you create margin as a cultivator, dial in operations, expand to a new market you don't know much about. You're not hiring a software person, you're hiring a seller or field marketer who uses software tools. I think the toolkit is going to get bigger for cannabis companies, and it's an exciting time for people like you guys, Lit Alerts, CanVersions, and a host of others.

Kellen Finney: I agree — it's easy to say bring someone in with software experience, but the moment you do, they need a team and resources. If you're already running a vertically integrated cannabis company with cultivation, retail, and extraction, essentially running four or five unrelated businesses, adding an in-house software build becomes an instant distraction from your core business, which is growing high-quality cannabis and selling the product. Tools become a luxury you buy to get better and faster, not build yourself. What do you think, Bryan?

Bryan Fields: I think we're all in agreement — it's the old adage of buy versus build. For outside-industry companies with 20,000 employees paying a few dollars a seat, those numbers add up fast enough that building in-house might make sense, which could disrupt other companies. But in cannabis, where resources are limited and companies are already dealing with endless challenges, adding another one in-house seems unnecessary. The bigger opportunity, like Lit Alerts and CanVersions, is finding a problem internally, building a solution for yourself first, and then recognizing it's applicable to the outside world — and tools like ChatGPT can help accelerate going from idea to MVP quickly, given how scrappy the industry already operates.

Rick Bashkoff: Agreed — and from an industry-value perspective, it's not efficient for all of us to be building our own software; it just adds to the lack of interoperability. The goal is competing on quality of product and service, not cornering customers. If we can hone in on that as an industry, maybe software doesn't have to be as expensive as it is today — if you're building the way we're building, the business model can be a lot friendlier. Look out for us pushing that envelope, because compared to software outside cannabis, some of what we pay a premium for here isn't as expensive elsewhere.

Bryan Fields: Love it. So for our listeners who want to get in touch and check out some of the products, where can they find you?

Rick Bashkoff: LitAlerts.com is the best place to check out Lit Alerts, and CanVersions.com as well. If you want resources on the investing side, go to ReceptiveCap.com, and feel free to reach out to me on LinkedIn too — I'm pretty active there, posting and engaging, kind of the home for cannabis business. Hit me up there, and we hope to hear from customers and new prospects alike.

Bryan Fields: Appreciate it, thanks for taking the time, this was a lot of fun.

Rick Bashkoff: Thank you.
summary: In this episode of The Dime, hosts Bryan Fields and Kellen Finney talk with Rick Bashkoff, a former music-industry and tech-startup operator turned cannabis investor and software executive, about why cannabis needs its own purpose-built software rather than one-size-fits-all solutions. Bashkoff shares his path from Warner Music Group to early-stage VC investing to running two cannabis-specific software products, Lit Alerts (competitive intelligence for brands, wholesalers, and retailers) and CanVersions (automated email marketing for dispensaries), explaining how founder-built, customer-driven tools are reshaping a fragmented, capital-constrained industry. The conversation also covers investing criteria for cannabis founders, the challenges of cannabis marketing regulation, and predictions for how AI and no-code tools will change staffing and software adoption across the industry.
takeaways: A 'second wave' of cannabis software companies is emerging, built lean and customer-driven rather than capital-heavy and all-in-one like earlier entrants.
Lit Alerts crawls dispensary menu websites hourly to generate real-time competitive intelligence on pricing, stock levels, and sales velocity for brands, wholesalers, and retailers.
CanVersions started as an internal tool built by a single-store dispensary operator (Bloom Brothers) to solve his own automated-email marketing needs before becoming a broader product.
Cannabis software's biggest operational difference from other industries is customer instability — collections issues, high churn, and constant disruption compared to enterprise software elsewhere.
Structured, clean data is a prerequisite for AI adoption in cannabis; without it, 'garbage in, garbage out' limits any AI-driven insight.
Investors like Receptive Capital Syndicate now prioritize founder grit, demonstrated resilience, and revenue traction over pitch decks or big-name comparisons like Facebook/Airbnb.
Cannabis marketing regulations remain a major constraint, creating tension between industry education goals and restrictive advertising rules that hinder competing with the illicit market.

Most cannabis operators are expected to partner with specialized software vendors rather than hire in-house software teams, since their core competency is growing and selling cannabis, not building tech.

faq.question: What problem does CanVersions solve for cannabis dispensaries?
faq.answer: CanVersions provides simple, automated, 'set-and-forget' email marketing for dispensaries — handling things like abandoned-cart follow-ups and win-back campaigns — so single-location operators with limited marketing resources don't need a full marketing team or complex enterprise tools.

faq.question: How does Lit Alerts gather its cannabis market data?
faq.answer: Lit Alerts uses a web crawler, similar to how Google indexes pages, to scan dispensary menu websites roughly every hour, comparing snapshots over time to infer real-time market activity such as low stock, out-of-stocks, and pricing changes.

faq.question: Why does the cannabis industry need software built specifically for it rather than generic tools?
faq.answer: Because cannabis operators face unique problems — unstable customers, compliance-driven marketing restrictions, fragmented data, and limited capital — generic enterprise software doesn't address these industry-specific pain points the way purpose-built cannabis tools can.

faq.question: What is Rick Bashkoff looking for when investing in cannabis founders through Receptive Capital Syndicate?
faq.answer: He prioritizes demonstrated grit and resilience in overcoming past challenges, a working and revenue-generating product rather than a pre-launch idea, and alignment with a team he trusts, rather than founders pitching purely on vision or big-name comparisons.

faq.question: What is the biggest operational difference between running a software company in cannabis versus outside of it?
faq.answer: According to Bashkoff, it's the stability of customers — cannabis software companies deal with far more collections issues, churn, and unpredictable disruptions than typical enterprise software businesses outside the industry.

faq.question: Will cannabis companies start hiring in-house software teams as AI tools like ChatGPT make development easier?
faq.answer: Bashkoff predicts the opposite — cannabis brands and retailers will increasingly partner with specialized software vendors rather than build in-house, since their core focus should remain growing, producing, and selling cannabis rather than managing software teams.

faq.question: What is the biggest challenge with cannabis marketing regulations today?
faq.answer: Regulations vary state by state and heavily restrict advertising and messaging, which conflicts with the industry's need to educate consumers and compete against the illicit market — a tension Bashkoff calls one of the biggest frustrations for cannabis marketers.

faq.question: Why does Rick Bashkoff believe cannabis beverages could be a major growth category?
faq.answer: He points out that grocery store shelves already have an entire regulated beverage section ready to be disrupted, unlike flower, pre-rolls, or gummies which aren't sold there, positioning cannabis beverages as a potential mainstream entry point.
